12.0.s.en: (1) Sanctifying the body and the mind for the spiritual life with God

12.0.0.en: The Apostle Paul directs the attention of the believers to the fact that, since God has dealt with them with all compassion, offering them salvation and redemption, they must in return, in order to keep these abundant blessings, present all their members to do good, righteousness and holiness, slay and drive out every evil desire that opposes this, and let the mind take part in praising and worshiping God.

12.1.0.en: The believer ought not to be conformed to the people of the world. How many behaviors or habits the world offers that contradict the commandment of Christ, and it even dares to accuse the Church and her children of being closed-minded and reactionary. Therefore we must not keep pace with the people of the world or please them, but let our minds and thoughts be enlightened every day by the thoughts of the Holy Bible, so that we may go from depth to depth in the spiritual life and become nearer to and more understanding of God's good will in our lives, and this is reflected in our outward conduct ("your form").

12.1.1.en: Know that you live in the world, but your principles are different from it. So do not share in its errors, and if you have been drawn along with it in some improper behaviors, you need repentance and the renewing of your mind, so that you may live for the love of God. Be strong in cutting off sin and everything that leads you to it, so that you may live occupied with the love of God.

12.2.s.en: (2) The kinds of gifts in the Church

12.2.0.en: St. Paul begins to explain the manner of service and the kinds of gifts in the Church, not as one speaking from himself, but under the guidance of the Holy Spirit within him.

12.2.1.en: May the servant always speak after praying to consult God, and not rush into speaking, relying on his own knowledge.

12.2.2.en: Then St. Paul says that the believer ought not to "think of himself more highly than he ought to think," that is, not to see himself, in conceit, as having great abilities beyond what is true, but to see himself as he truly is, so that he may recognize what gift God has given him and work with it in faith. For the work of service is built essentially on trust in the work of God, however weak a person's abilities may be.

12.3.0.en: Our God is a God of order. He made the members of His Church like the members of one body, each one having a specific role and a specific function different from the other's yet complementing it. The gifts given to each member of the Church are meant to serve others, not for personal boasting.

12.4.0.en: The grace of the Holy Spirit determines, with great wisdom, for each person the gift he will receive according to his personal readiness to receive it. The gifts are not divided into great kinds and small kinds, because the Church needs all the gifts with the same importance, so no one should look at his brother's gift and covet it. These gifts are:

12.4.1.en: First, prophecy: it is the revealing of heavenly mysteries and future events, and among the most famous of these prophecies is the Book of Revelation of St. John the Beloved. The Holy Spirit gives this gift if He finds faith in the speaker and the listener.

12.4.2.en: In the New Testament, the future is the Kingdom of Heaven, so speaking about it, that is, about our relationship with God and how He reigns over our lives in preparation for eternity, is another meaning of prophecy.

12.5.0.en: Second, ministry: this differs from social services in that it essentially has a lofty goal, which is to bring the one served to the Lord Christ.

12.5.1.en: Third, teaching: this is different from prophesying, for it is the explanation and simplification of the truths of faith and theological matters so that the simple person served may understand them.

12.5.2.en: We note that every believer must stay with his gift and not go beyond its field into the field of another gift. For this reason St. Paul repeats his saying, with the gift in the same kind of gift, such as "he that ministereth, on ministering."

12.6.0.en: Fourth, exhortation: this is advising others and guiding them how to walk in the path of virtue and to behave as befits children of God. Thus the teacher addresses the mind while the exhorter addresses the heart and the will, so that both may move the body and soul toward holy spiritual conduct.

12.6.1.en: Giving: this speaks of the virtues that he wants all believers to enjoy, unlike the gifts that are given to only some. The virtues are necessary for a person's salvation, while the gifts are for the service of the Church. Giving in the world's understanding is tied to expecting something in return, such as a wage or reward, but giving in the Church is with liberality, that is, in abundance and without expecting anything in return, to the point that a person offers his whole self to others.

12.6.2.en: Then he returns, a second time, to the gifts and speaks about:

12.6.3.en: Fifth, ruling with diligence: ruling is the organizing, arranging and distributing of responsibilities in the ministry, and guiding, directing and supporting everyone. And why diligence? Because Church matters must be taken with seriousness, depth and wise thought, not hasty or superficial. The ruler is diligent, that is, he is not content with the role of adviser, but works in the field of service with his own hands and shares with others in their work and labors.

12.6.4.en: Then he continues his long discourse on the virtues and speaks to us about mercy, which in the world's understanding is only exempting the wrongdoer from punishment, whereas spiritual mercy is cheerfulness, that is, showing love, warmth and heartfelt forgiveness to the wrongdoer, and accepting him as a living, active member serving in the Church.

12.6.5.en: If we are members of one body, then may you value the service of every person, however small it may seem, and encourage him with kind words. At the same time, do not despise any small work that you offer, confident that God cares about it. And if you are doing a great service, do not become proud, because it is a grace given to you for the sake of others, lest God withdraw it from you, however gifted you are, in order to save you from your pride.

12.7.0.en: Love: how many relationships in this world are classed under the title of love, such as emotional love in words only without any self-giving, and love that expects something in return for a personal interest or benefit. All of these are certainly unacceptable before God, and therefore they are called hypocritical love.

12.7.1.en: But true love without hypocrisy is that which springs from the heart in limitless self-giving, and this has an abundant reward from God. The one who has this love finds himself hating every evil. For we cannot do evil except to one whom we hate, and when we love a person, we find that we do all possible good for him with wonderful spontaneity. Therefore love has become inseparable from doing good.

12.8.0.en: Kindly affection: this is different from the world's "courtesy," in which people flatter one another in various ways that are all formal. True kindly affection springs from a loving heart, showing itself in offering and honoring the other. The word "kindly affectioned" means that we take the initiative in showing affection to others, so that we are not only receivers of affection.

12.9.0.en: We must be diligent: to acquire the virtues, and when God sees our striving, He rewards us with spiritual fervor and zeal in our relationship with Him, so that we worship Him sincerely. The reverse is also true: when we worship the Lord and pray to Him much, the fervor of the Spirit is kindled in us, and this leads us to diligence in spiritual matters and practical virtues without laziness.

12.10.0.en: Patience and hope during tribulation: on our journey toward eternity many tribulations confront us, whose aim is to hinder us, wound us and make us fall. Therefore St. Paul offers the solution, which is rejoicing in hope, that is, looking to the glory that is about to be revealed in us. For tribulation is our field for gain and for winning the heavenly reward, if we succeed and persevere in prayer, as though we were saying that nothing separates us from the love of Christ, and so we find great help and strength from God supporting us.

12.11.0.en: Giving to the needy and the stranger: and how beautiful is the title that St. Paul gave to the poor, for they are the saints because of the hardship of life they endure, and the injustice of the rich and the harshness of the proud toward them. He also means by the saints the believers who are sanctified in Christ. The word "distributing" means that every member of the body must share in this service to his needy brother. Therefore the early Church lived a life called the "life of fellowship," in which there were no natural differences, for all were satisfied.

12.11.1.en: "Given to hospitality": the word "given" means constant care for these strangers. And strangers are not only those who need to be cared for materially, but also psychologically, for many suffer from isolation and a feeling of loneliness, either because people are too busy for them or because of their moving from one country to another, and they need someone who shows them care and love.

12.12.0.en: Blessing those who wrong us: here St. Paul raises us step by step to the summit of the mountain of the commandments, which is dealing with those who wrong us. His commandment "curse not" may be acceptable, but how can I bless and pray for good for one who persecutes me, wrongs me and takes away my rights?! The answer is that sin is weakness, so the one who persecutes me has fallen under the hand of the devil, and I must pray for him that God may rescue him, and praying for him changes his heart so that he becomes a member like us in the Church, as happened with St. Paul himself. And I bless the persecutor, because his persecutions will become medals on my chest before Christ. In wars of old, the brave soldier felt proud of his wounds and his amputated limbs, which he bore with honor.

12.12.1.en: In sum, we have compassion on those who wrong us because sin is weakness, we accept tribulation from the hand of God because it is for our good, and we overflow with the divine love dwelling in us, so we bless them and pray for them.

12.13.0.en: Then St. Paul directs us to share in the other's joy, that is, to rejoice for him from my heart without jealousy and without envy, and my sharing in the expressions of his joy must be within limits that do not grieve the Spirit of Christ dwelling in me. Although the person in the world today refuses to share in the other's sorrow because he simply cannot bear the other or even listen to his sorrows and cares, the spiritual person is always a tender bosom, a listening ear and a gentle, comforting tongue.

12.14.0.en: Humility: our sharing with one another in joy and sorrow makes us one body with one concern, which is eternal life, not concerned with the material things of the world and the grandeur of living ("high things"), but it leads us to be drawn to the lowly, that is, to imitate the humble saints and follow their example. Among the virtues of the humble person is that he listens, learns, obeys and submits, whereas the proud "wise man" is the one who walks according to his personal desires and opinions, not submitting to guides or priests or the Church or even God Himself. True wisdom is in submission to God and to guides, whereas the one who is wise in his own eyes is the proud, so his wisdom is false and mere cleverness or information, but he cannot act well, because wisdom is good conduct.

12.15.0.en: The Lord Christ abolished the idea of repaying the other in kind, that is, evil for evil, because the believer's nature has become love for everyone, even those who wrong him. Not only that, but the Christian must not be a cause of stumbling by any wrong conduct of his before people, but must always act with propriety, courtesy and gentleness, so that the world may see the good image of the children of God and glorify Him.

12.16.0.en: "Live peaceably": this means that I, as a Christian, strive to make peace, which is reconciliation with all people with a pure heart, on my own initiative, and I do not wait for the other to come to me. The peacemaker is a positive person, not weak or passive.

12.16.1.en: And why did St. Paul say "as much as lieth in you"?

12.16.2.en: Because there are people who may refuse to make peace with me without any cause from me, merely because I am a Christian or because of some evil in their hearts, and here I am innocent of this quarrel, which is on their side only, while my heart is open to loving them even if they insist on boycotting me.

12.17.0.en: Without doubt the wronged soul fights with anger and the desire for revenge, and here St. Paul, like a wise physician, directs the believer to a psychologically and spiritually healthy way of dealing with this anger and this desire for revenge, saying, "give place unto wrath," that is, let God be angry in your place, and in His anger He will avenge you, for God is just and He alone has the right to repay because He is without sin. So we leave God, the wise Father, to discipline and teach His children what is good, while I pray for those who wronged me, and in this our resentment toward the wrongdoer ends, and there will be no room for gloating over him if the hand of God stretches out to discipline him; on the contrary, he is then in a position that calls for pity for him because of God's vengeance.

12.18.0.en: Therefore if you know that your enemy is hungry and in need, give to him and help him, or if he is thirsty, give him drink. In this you will force him to be ashamed of himself, and he will review his conscience, rebuke himself and repent, as though by your love you had put a fire burning in his head, burning up his wrong thoughts toward you, so that he returns and loves you.

12.19.0.en: That is the means of overcoming evil, not by answering it with evil but by doing good. We overcome the proud with our humility, the angry with our gentle words, and the thief with our embracing him.

12.19.1.en: You, beloved, are called to acquire all these virtues so that you may truly become a son of God, and their sum is that you love every person, feel his need and strive to help him. And in proportion to your practical love you receive inner peace and a blessing from God in all your steps.

12.19.2.en: The duties of the Christian in society, and his repentance

13.0.s.en: (1) The duties of the Christian toward society

13.0.0.en: Christianity lived, in most of its ages, under the rule of non-Christians, and here St. Paul points out that authority is good in general, because it is a social order for regulating life and relations among people, and this is better than primitive societies dominated by chaos and the rule of gangs. God rejoices in authority because He is a God of order and not a God of confusion, for authority is an arrangement that God approves for ordering society, and the Apostle commands us to submit to it and respond to it.

13.1.0.en: Whoever resists authority, that is, rejects it, opposes it and fights it, is as though he resists God Himself, and also exposes himself to earthly judgment, that is, the punishment of the rulers. Even in the ages when rulers resisted and persecuted the Christians, what was required was submission, which reached the point of martyrdom, which was by God's permission since it was a cause of blessing and of the spread of Christianity. Therefore Christianity, throughout its ages, did not allow revolutions or riots against the states or authorities that persecuted it, but endured the persecutions with bravery, courage and joy.

13.2.0.en: We return once more to ordinary systems of government, that is, those that do not persecute Christianity, where the Saint says that government and rulers are not a terror or a punishment to those who do good, but a cause of fear and discipline for evildoers, such as thieves, murderers, bribe-takers, forgers, and so on. Therefore whoever wants to live in peace under any system of government should do good, that is, what is required of him or permitted by the laws of the state, and so become a good citizen.

13.3.0.en: "The sword": punishing the wicked by death.

13.3.1.en: The one in authority is a minister of God, whom He established to judge justly among people, so that security, justice and tranquility prevail in society, and thus society is purified. For this reason St. Paul gives advice to everyone who does evil, so that:

13.3.2.en: First, he may not enter the circle of fear, anxiety and punishment from the rulers.

13.3.3.en: Second, because our Christian conscience, which loves humility, obedience and self-giving, is satisfied with nothing but carrying out the commandment of Christ to submit to the authorities. Christianity is a peaceful religion, not an objecting, resisting or troublemaking one. This does not mean that a person should not demand his right or defend it, but let him demand his right by sound, logical ways and not by crooked methods or illogical argument. For in the ages of persecution great defenders appeared who defended the Christian religion with all their strength.

13.3.4.en: If we are required to submit to our unbelieving rulers in the world, how much more should we submit to our spiritual shepherds, such as priests and guides, and to our fathers and mothers.

13.4.0.en: If the Christian submits to the authorities in everything that does not conflict with God's commandments, it is obvious that this means submission in simple matters such as paying tribute, that is, taxes, because they pay for public services for the whole society. And although the Church has blessed giving to the needy ("the necessity of saints"), she counts the tax collectors as God's ministers who collect contributions to serve others, as well as the public services that all citizens enjoy.

13.5.0.en: "Tribute": a tax on persons or property, given to the collectors of tribute.

13.5.1.en: "Custom": a tax on trade goods, given to the collectors of custom.

13.5.2.en: The Lord Christ Himself gave us an example when He paid the tribute and said, "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which be Caesar's, and unto God the things which be God's" (Lk 20:25). Everyone must receive his due, and we must show respect to everyone in a position, with esteem and fear and not out of hypocrisy or opportunism, so that we fear evil and do not do it out of fear of its punishment, and likewise we honor those in positions in the state with the customary honor for these ranks, so we confirm our agreement with and submission to the order of society, which is useful for keeping everything in check.

13.5.3.en: You, beloved, should review your stance toward your superiors, and ask yourself.

13.5.4.en: 1- Am I faithful in what is required of me, or am I lazy and negligent in my work?

13.5.5.en: 2- Do I demand my right by upright ways if I am wronged, or do I perhaps resort to crooked or violent ways to take my right?

13.6.s.en: (2) Loving every person in the world

13.6.0.en: The Apostle Paul commands the Christian to love others in society, because God has put overflowing love in the heart of every Christian to distribute it to others as though it were a debt on him that he is bound to pay to others, because the Christian is the light of the world, a refuge for everyone weary and a tender bosom for everyone in need of love. The Christian must not owe anything to anyone, that is, take something material or moral from people and not return it, because in this he would be like a thief.

13.6.1.en: The Law is divided into two parts:

13.6.2.en: a) A part concerning commandments toward God.

13.6.3.en: b) A part concerning commandments toward people (Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, and so on), and the sum of it is that you love your neighbor as yourself. Note that the Lord Christ interpreted the meaning of the neighbor, in the parable of the Good Samaritan, as any person in need in the world.

13.7.0.en: Whoever loves someone cannot do him harm, and the one who has love finds that he does not sin against any of the commandments of the Law, that is, he is perfect in all the commandments of the Law, for love is the fulfilling of the Law.

13.7.1.en: Therefore, beloved, if you have fallen into many sins, or are failing in your spiritual exercises to resist sin, know that the easiest and shortest way to obtain the virtues is love. Purify your heart from resentment and hatred, and then the virtues will flow into your heart one by one until perfection.

13.8.s.en: (3) Repentance now, before time is lost

13.8.0.en: The Apostle Paul warns us not to waste time in the pleasures of the world or in vain things, for we do not know how much of our life remains. Every day that passes brings us closer to meeting Christ, and death may come to us sooner than we imagine, or Christ Himself may come in His Second Coming at any time. So let us rise and leave the works of darkness, which are evils, and do the works of light, which are the virtues. He likened virtue to armor because of its power for victory over the enemy's attacks.

13.8.1.en: He likens our life on earth to the night for the darkness, gloom and weariness in it, and our meeting with Christ in Paradise to the joyful, happy day.

13.8.2.en: Note, beloved, the beauty of the verse "The night is far spent," for it gives comfort to everyone weary that every evil and injustice will soon pass away. So endure with thanksgiving from the hand of God, confident of the eternal reward, and you will also receive peace and comfort on earth.

13.9.1.en: "Chambering and wantonness": all kinds of adultery and perversion.

13.9.2.en: Let us walk in fitting works and good conduct as though we were in the day, that is, as though everyone sees us. It is not right for us to indulge in evil desires. It is strange that he added strife and envying after grave sins like adultery, to make clear that all of them deprive us of the Kingdom.

13.9.3.en: One of the gentle exercises for leaving sin is to ask myself:

13.9.4.en: Would I have done this sin if people were seeing me now? And the more important question: can I do this sin while God sees me now?

13.9.5.en: So train yourself to be aware of God's presence, as Elijah the prophet says, "As the Lord liveth, before whom I stand" (1 Kgs 17:1), and by this you will keep away from every sin.

13.10.0.en: "Provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof": the inclination and planning to carry out evil desires and the body's indulgence in worldly pleasures.

13.10.1.en: But the greatest means of overcoming sin is to "put on the Lord Jesus Christ," that is, always meditating on the life of the Lord Jesus, following the conduct of Christ, being united with Him and abiding in Him in the sacrament of the Eucharist, and being satisfied with His love, tenderness and care, and in this we will not find in ourselves an inclination to the lusts of the flesh, and we will not be able to anger God. Caring for the weak in faith and not causing them to stumble
